podcast.title: Brought to Stax by Joe Galkin
podcast.body: Johnny Jenkins, a local guitarist, was brought to Stax by record promoter Joe Galkin, who hoped Stax could help him achieve an instrumental hit, given the label's success with such tracks. "Joe Galkin, a record promoter to whom Jim Stewart Oda Favour was merging a local guitarist, Johnny Jenkins, and brought him into the studio to see if Stax could get him an instrumental hit"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Otis Redding's Driver
podcast.body: Jenkins could not drive, so his band's singer, Otis Redding, drove him to the Stax studio for his session. This circumstance serendipitously led to Redding's own recording opportunity. "Galkin had made a deal with the singer in Jenkins's band. If he'd drive Jenkins to the studio, since Jenkins couldn't drive, he'd try to get a record cut with him as well."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Unsuccessful Stax Single
podcast.body: Jenkins did release a single on Stax, but it was not particularly special and failed to achieve any success. His first session at Stax was considered a flop. "Jenkins did eventually release a single on Stax, but it wasn't particularly special and didn't have any success. The day of Jenkins's first session was a flop."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Live Recording Sampled by Beastie Boys
xref.body: A "quick squawk" from a live Jimi Hendrix recording from 1969 was sampled and used in the Beastie Boys' 1992 song "Pass the Mic." This illustrates the use of live performance snippets in sampling, adding dynamic and recognizable elements to new compositions. "After a quick squawk from alive Jimmy Hendrix recording from 1969, we end up at a sample of a 1970 track called I Walk on Gilded Splinters from Johnny Jenkins at around the three minute and fifteen second market of the song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
